meta.title: Directive 2010/64/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 October 2010 on the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings

items.heading: Article 1
items.comment: The Act on Strengthening the Procedural Rights of Defendants in Criminal Proceedings (Gesetz zur Stärkung der Verfahrensrechte von Beschuldigten im Strafverfahren) was issued to implement the Directives 2010/64 and 2012/13 into the German CCP and CCA and entered into effect on 6th July 2013. The legislator has predominantly refrained from a literal implementation of the fundamental right to interpretation and translation as laid down in the Directive, since, in his opinion, the prevailing law already guaranteed most of the rights to be implemented. Instead he has mainly opted for an addition to the wording of already existing provisions on the basis of their previous interpretation by case law and introduced only few new provisions.

items.text: 1. This Directive lays down rules concerning the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings and proceedings for the execution of a European arrest warrant.

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: A transposition of this specific article is considered dispensable, as this is simply a description of the subject area.

items.text: 2. The right referred to in paragraph 1 shall apply to persons from the time that they are made aware by the competent authorities of a Member State, by official notification or otherwise, that they are suspected or accused of having committed a criminal offence until the conclusion of the proceedings, which is understood to mean the final determination of the question whether they have committed the offence, including, where applicable, sentencing and the resolution of any appeal.

provisions.comment: Article 185 (1) 1 sentence only applies to the court hearing
provisions.textEn: If the trial is conducted with the participation of persons who have no command of the German language, an interpreter must be called in.

1 The court shall provide an interpreter or a translator for an accused or convicted person who has no command of the German language insofar as this is necessary for the exercise of his rights under the law of criminal procedure. 2 The court shall advise the accused in a language he understands that he may to this extent demand that an interpreter or a translator be called in for the entire criminal proceedings free of charge.

The communication with a hearing impaired or speech impaired person shall, at their choice, be oral, written or with the assistance of a person enabling the communication, who shall be called in by the court.

items.comment:
The temporal scope of the right to interpretation and translation beyond the main hearing is only implicitly expressed: by the denomination of the protected person in section 187 (1) 1 Court Constitution Act (CCA) and the obligation to inform him/her that he/she is entitled to the free assistance of an interpreter or translator throughout the criminal proceedings in section 187 (1) 2 CCA. (The right of interpretation and translation was already previously contained in sections 185 (1) and 187 (1) 1 CCA and only the provision on the obligation to provide information in Section 187 (1) 2 CCA was created in transposition of the Directive, which is why de facto/indirectly implementation was chosen.)


The beginning of the protection is indicated by the use of the word 'Beschuldigter', who in German criminal procedure is a person initially suspected of a crime, against whom the law enforcement authorities are conducting an investigation. When they are made aware by the competent authorities, that they are suspected or accused, they also benefit from the rights to interpretation and translation. This lays down the scope of the right from the investigative stage on to the final judgment.

The end of the protection is marked by the use of the word 'Verurteilter', a person convicted by a final judgment. Thus, German law grants the accused person the right only until the conclusion of the ordinary appeal proceedings, but no longer in proceedings on extraordinary legal remedies such as application for retrial and constitutional complaint, which is considered insufficient in the literature (Schneider, Strafverteidiger 2015, 379, 380 et seq). Literature also endorse the endorse the applicability of the provision during the enforcement proceedings following a judgment (Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para. 9; Rosenau, in: Satzger/Schluckebier/Widmaier, Strafprozessordnung, 4th ed. 2020, § 187 GVG para. 1).


With regards to persons with hearing or speech impairments, section 186 CCA states that communication is to be made orally, in writing or with the assistance of a person who can be called in by the court. According to its systematic context, the provision is directly applicable only to court proceedings (see the legislative materials on the amendment of the provision in 2017, BT-Drs. 18/10144, p. 30). It is generally acknowledged that the corresponding rights also apply in the investigative stage as well as in enforcement proceedings (instead of many Diemer, in: Karlsruher Kommentar zur Strafprozessordnung, 8th ed. 2019, § 186 GVG para. 1); this also corresponds to the will of the legislature when drafting the provision (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 14/9266, p. 41). However, a corresponding statutory provision is missing.

items.text: 3. Where the law of a Member State provides for the imposition of a sanction regarding minor offences by an authority other than a court having jurisdiction in criminal matters, and the imposition of such a sanction may be appealed to such a court, this Directive shall apply only to the proceedings before that court following such an appeal.

provisions.comment:
The Administrative Offences Act does not contain any explicit guarantee of the rights contained in the Directive. Instead, by way of a general reference, the provisions of the CCP are declared to be applicable mutatis mutandis.

This implementation does not appear to be sufficiently clear and precise.
provisions.textEn: (1) Unless otherwise provided by this Act, the provisions of general statutes concerning criminal proceedings, particularly those of the Code of Criminal Procedure, of the Courts Constitution Act and of the Youth Court Act, shall apply mutatis mutandis to the regulatory fining proceedings.

items.text: 4. This Directive does not affect national law concerning the presence of legal counsel during any stage of the criminal proceedings, nor does it affect national law concerning the right of access of a suspected or accused person to documents in criminal proceedings.

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: No need for implementation apparent. There is no indication that the implementation of the Directive has led to a limitation of the rights mentioned.

items.heading: Article 2

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that suspected or accused persons who do not speak or understand the language of the criminal proceedings concerned are provided, without delay, with interpretation during criminal proceedings before investigative and judicial authorities, including during police questioning, all court hearings and any necessary interim hearings.

provisions.textEn: If the trial is conducted with the participation of persons who have no command of the German language, an interpreter must be called in.

The court will call in an interpreter or a translator for an accused or convicted person who has no command of the German language, insofar as this is necessary for the exercise of his procedural rights in criminal proceedings.

provisions.comment: Art. 163a (5) CCP was introduced by the Act on strengthening the procedural rights of defendants in criminal proceedings (Gesetz zur Stärkung der Verfahrensrechte von Beschuldigten im Strafverfahren), which was issued to implement the Directives 2010/64 and 2012/13 into the German CCP and CCA. However, since it is only considered to be a clarification, 'de facto implementation' was chosen.
provisions.textEn: Section 187 paragraphs 1 to 3 and Section 189 paragraph 4 of the Court Constitution Act apply accordingly.

An accused person who does not have command of the language of the court must be informed by the interpreter of at least the motions of the public prosecutor and the defence counsel from the final speeches.

items.comment:
Before 2004, the right to the use of an interpreter was only explicitly regulated in section 185 GVG for the main hearing, whereas the corresponding right for interrogations in investigative proceedings was derived from Art. 6 (3) e ECHR. In the opinion of the legislator, with regards to the suspected person the introduction of section 187 (1) CCA in 2004 (now Subsection 1, Sentence 1, Court Constitution Act) only served the purpose of clarification (legislative materials, BR-Drs. 829/03, p. 45). The same applies to the introduction of the reference in Section 163a (5) CCP regarding interrogations by the police and public prosecutor's office in investigative proceedings to the provision for the main hearing in implementation of Art. 1, 2 and 5 (3) of the Directive 2010/64/EU as well as Art. 3 (1) d of the Directive 2012/13/EU (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 17/12578, p. 8; Griesbaum, in: Karlsruher Kommentar zur, Strafprozessordnung, 8th ed. 2019, § 163a para. 30b).


However, the Directive fully guarantees the right during the whole criminal proceedings before investigative and judicial authorities and makes it subject to a reservation only in Art. 1(2) with regards to the contact between defendant and defence counsel. German law, on the other hand, only guarantees it unconditionally for the court hearing in section 185 GVG and otherwise only 'insofar as this is necessary for the exercise of his procedural rights in criminal proceedings' (more details below). However, in the literature it is assumed that this requirement is always met, especially so that the accused can communicate with his defence counsel (Eisenberg, Juristische Rundschau 2013, 442, 445; Frister, in: Systematischer Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 9, 5th ed. 2016, § 187 GVG para. 2; Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para. 9). Whether this also corresponds to practice cannot be assessed.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that, where necessary for the purpose of safeguarding the fairness of the proceedings, interpretation is available for communication between suspected or accused persons and their legal counsel in direct connection with any questioning or hearing during the proceedings or with the lodging of an appeal or other procedural applications.

provisions.textEn: If the trial is conducted with the participation of persons who have no command of the German language, an interpreter must be called in.

The court will call in an interpreter or a translator for an accused or convicted person who has no command of the German language, insofar as this is necessary for the exercise of his procedural rights in criminal proceedings.
Art. 187 (1) to (3) and Art. 189 (4) of the Court Constitution Act apply accordingly.

items.comment: As explained above, German law only guarantees the right to interpretation and translation outside the main hearing 'insofar as this is necessary for the exercise of his procedural rights in criminal proceedings' and has thus opted for a wording which differs from that of the Directive. The wording of the Directive tends to appear broader and the differences in the wording also give rise to the risk of different interpretations (see also the criticism by Oğla﻿kcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para. 7).

items.text: 3. The right to interpretation under paragraphs 1 and 2 includes appropriate assistance for persons with hearing or speech impediments.

provisions.textEn:
(1) Communication with a hearing-impaired or speech-impaired person during the hearing shall, at his choice, take place orally, in writing or with the assistance of a communication facilitator to be called in by the court. The court shall furnish suitable technical aids for oral and written communication. The hearing-impaired or speech-impaired person shall be advised of his right to choose.

(2) The court may require written communication or order a person to be called in as an interpreter if the hearing-impaired or speech-impaired person has not availed himself of his right to choose pursuant to subsection (1) or if adequate communication is not possible in the form chosen pursuant to subsection (1) or would require disproportionate effort.

(3) The Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection shall specify in a statutory instrument, which shall require the approval of the Bundesrat,

1. the extent of the right to provision of appropriate communication aids pursuant to subsections (1) and (2),

2. the principles of appropriate remuneration for the use of communication aids pursuant to subsections (1) and (2),

3. the appropriate communication aids by means of which the communication specified in subsections (1) and (2) is to be guaranteed, and

4. whether and how the person with a hearing or speech impairment is required to cooperate.

items.comment: Regarding the temporal scope of the provision see above (commentary on the implementation of Art. 1 (2))

items.text: 4. Member States shall ensure that a procedure or mechanism is in place to ascertain whether suspected or accused persons speak and understand the language of the criminal proceedings and whether they need the assistance of an interpreter.

nationalActs.title: Richtlinien für das Strafverfahren und das Bußgeldverfahren
nationalActs.titleEn: Directives on criminal and administrative fine proceedings

provisions.textEn: At the first examination of an foreing accused of foreign nationality, a record shall be kept of whether the accused has a sufficient command of the German language that an interpreter need not be called in.

items.comment:
The provisions on the use of interpreters in (criminal) proceedings presuppose inadequate command of languages, but do not establish a mechanism for determining language skills. Only the Directives on criminal and administrative fine proceedings (Richtlinien für das Strafverfahren und das Bußgeldverfahren, RiStBV) contain the requirement to record, when questioning a foreign accused, whether the accused has sufficient language skills that no interpreter needs to be called in (section 181, see below). Yet, the RiStBV are administrative regulations without legal force. They are issued by the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, are primarily aimed at the public prosecutor's office and the police and are intended to ensure a uniform approach in the relevant procedures.


However, since the use of an interpreter without establishing the lack of language command is hardly conceivable, it is recognised in case-law and literature that the Court has to assess language proficiency of its own motion, but how it does so is left to its discretion (BGHSt 3, 285; BGH NStZ 1984, 328; OLG Stuttgart, NJW 2006, 3796, 3798; Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 185 para. 6). According to the prevailing opinion, the use of interpreters in borderline cases and their scope is left to the discretion of the court as well; however, this is criticised in the literature, since either the command of the language was insufficient and the use of an interpreter therefore fully necessary and unrestrictedly ordered in section 185 CCA or not (Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 185 GVG para. 37).


A test of language skills is therefore carried out in practice and is necessarily required by law, but is not explicitly prescribed there. The recognition of discretion does not guarantee that the respective test by the court will be carried out reliably and that a required translator will be called in in every case.

items.text: 5. Member States shall ensure that, in accordance with procedures in national law, suspected or accused persons have the right to challenge a decision finding that there is no need for interpretation and, when interpretation has been provided, the possibility to complain that the quality of the interpretation is not sufficient to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings.

provisions.textEn: The rules on exclusion and rejection of experts shall apply to the interpreter accordingly.

provisions.comment: The law thus refers to sections 22 to 24 CCP on the exclusion of a judge on the grounds of partiality.
provisions.textEn:
(1) An expert may be challenged on the same grounds as those on which a judge is challenged. [...]

 (2) 1 [...] the accused shall have the right of challenge.
Against the judgments of the criminal judge (“Strafrichter”) and the Court of lay assessors (“Schöffengericht”) an (appeal) “Berufung” may be lodged.

Appeals on points of law (“Revision”) may be lodged against the judgments of the “Strafkammern” and the “Schwurgericht” (i.e. Regional Court), as well as against the judgments of the higher regional courts handed down at first instance.

A judgment must always be considered to be based on an infringement of the law, [...]

No. 5     if the main hearing took place in the absence of the prosecution or a person whose presence is required by law [...].

A complaint shall be admissible against all orders made by the courts of first instance or in proceedings on an appeal on points of fact and law and against directions given by the presiding judge, the judge in the preliminary investigation, and by a commissioned or a requested judge, unless such orders are expressly exempted from appellate remedy by law.

items.comment:
Since the interpreter, like an expert, is considered an assistant of the court, he or she can be excluded or refused on the grounds of partiality, section 191 Courts Constitution Act in conjunction with section 74 Code of Criminal Procedure.


The usual legal remedies are open to the suspect in cases of violation of the rules on interpretation and translation. 

In preliminary proceedings, it is also the court with jurisdiction for the main proceedings that decides whether an interpreter and, if so, which one should be called in. Against this decision the accused may lodge an complaint (Beschwerde) according to section 304 CCP.

However, the decision not to call in an interpreter is not subject to a complaint if it precedes the judgement of the court hearing the case on the merits, serves to prepare this judgement and has no effect beyond the judgement. In these cases he must appeal the judgment.

In the case of accusations of minor weight, which at first instance fall within the jurisdiction of the district court (Amtsgericht), he may lodge an appeal ('Berufung'), section 312 CCP, which will lead to a new main hearing in the next instance. This appeal is open to the accused irrespective of whether an error of law has occurred.

In these, but also in all other cases, he may file an appeal on points of law ('Revision'), section 333 CCP, which leads to a review of errors of law and only exceptionally includes a hearing. In principle, an appeal will only be successful if the judgment is based on an error of law, i.e. if there is at least the possibility that the outcome would have been different had the proceedings been free of errors of law. However, the absence of a translator required by law during the main trial represents a so-called absolute revision ground according to section 338 Nr. 5 CCP, which means that it is legally presumed that the error has influenced the judgment. In the case of other errors, such as absence of an interpreter in the investigative proceedings, poor quality of the interpretation or partial absence of the interpreter, the above-mentioned correlation between the procedural error and the judgment must appear possible; furthermore, those decisions which are at the discretion of the court are not subject to review by the Court of Appeal, e.g. the choice of the specific translator, the assessment of the language command and the use of an interpreter in borderline cases, see commentary on Art. 2 (4).

That there is no direct possibility to challenge a decision denying the need for interpretation during the investigative proceddings, is considered unproblematic by Mansdörfer/Schmitt, since due to the principles of immediacy and orality, the questioning will be repeated at the main trial and the statement from the pre-trial proceedings could not be used (in: Allegrezza/Covolo (eds.), Effective Defence Rights in Criminal Proceedings, 2018, p. 295, 315).

items.text: 6. Where appropriate, communication technology such as videoconferencing, telephone or the Internet may be used, unless the physical presence of the interpreter is required in order to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings.

provisions.comment: The provision does not contain the express reservation regarding the requirement of presence for reasons of fairness. However, it grants the court discretion, the exercise of which must take into account the need for direct communication.
provisions.textEn: 1The Court may permit the interpreter to be present elsewhere during the trial, hearing or examination. 2 The trial, hearing or examination shall be simultaneously transmitted in sound and vision to that place and to the courtroom.

items.comment: The use of videoconferencing technology is regulated in section 185 (1a) CCA and thus only for the main hearing. For hearings in investigative proceedings, such a practice is considered permissible anyways (see the legislative materials, BT-Drs. 17/1224, p. 10; Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 185 GVG para. 8a). The possibility of section 185a (1a) CCA is rarely used in practice, as direct communication is deemed necessary (Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 185 GVG para. 8a).

items.text: 7. In proceedings for the execution of a European arrest warrant, the executing Member State shall ensure that its competent authorities provide persons subject to such proceedings who do not speak or understand the language of the proceedings with interpretation in accordance with this Article.

nationalActs.title: Gesetz über die internationale Rechtshilfe in Strafsachen
nationalActs.titleEn: Act on International Cooperation in Criminal Matters

provisions.comment:
The legislator of the Act on Strengthening the Procedural Rights of Defendants in Criminal Proceedings assumed that through the provision of section 77 IRG a level of protection beyond that of the Directive would be achieved. The reference to section 187 CCA not only required a translation of the European arrest warrant, as the directive stipulates, but also other written procedural documents in the extradition proceedings.


However, Schneider (Strafverteidiger 2013, 379, 381) considers this general reference to the rules on criminal procedure insufficient for three reasons. The provision of section 187 CCA applicable to the EAW only addresses courts, but not the Ministry of Justice, which is responsible for receiving EAW; moreover, until recently, EAW were approved by the Prosecutor General's Office. Furthermore, it is considered doubtful whether the mutatis mutandis reference to sectin 187 CCA, which refers to the rights of criminal procedure, meets the requirements of certainty for the implementation of the Directive. Finally, the European Arrest Warrant is not covered by the presumption of section 187 (1) 1 CCA; its translation is therefore subject to the court's scope of assessment under paragraph 1.
provisions.textEn: (1) In the absence of special procedural rules provided for under this Act, the provisions of the Courts Constitution Act and of the Introductory Act to the Courts Constitution Act (Einführungsgesetz zum Gerichtsverfassungsgesetz), of the Code of Criminal Procedure, of the Youth Courts Act, of the Fiscal Code (Abgabenordnung) and of the Act on Regulatory Offences (Gesetz über Ordnungswidrigkeiten) apply analogously.

items.text: 8. Interpretation provided under this Article shall be of a quality sufficient to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings, in particular by ensuring that suspected or accused persons have knowledge of the case against them and are able to exercise their right of defence.

provisions.textEn:
(1) 1The interpreter has to take an oath to this effect:

   that he will translate faithfully and conscientiously.[...]

(2) If the interpreter is generally sworn in for translations of the respective kind according to the Court Interpreters Act or in a Land according to the federel regulations, it is sufficient to refer to this oath before all courts of the Federation and the federal states.

nationalActs.title: Gesetz über die allgemeine Beeidigung von gerichtlichen Dolmetschern

provisions.textEn: Interpreters who are to be called in under section 185 of the Judicial System Act [...] for language transmission in court hearings shall be sworn in in accordance with the provisions of this Act.

(1) As a court interpreter for one or more languages, the following persons shall be sworn on request [...]

3. is suitable, […]

5. is reliable, and

6. has the necessary language skills.

(2) Anyone who has passed one of the following examinations is considered to have the necessary language skills referred to in paragraph 1(6):

1. in Germany, the interpreting examination of a state or state-recognised examination office or university or

2. abroad, an interpreter examination recognised by a competent German body as equivalent to an examination pursuant to point 1.
alternative certificate of competence

items.comment:
The appointment of an interpreter by the court, in practice as a rule after selection from a court interpreter and translator database (http://www.justiz-dolmetscher.de/, as of 13th April 2020), as well as his or her swearing in in accordance with section 189 (1) CCA and the punishability of a wilfully false translation are regarded as measures to ensure the quality of the translation service. At present, the general swearing-in of interpreters and translators leading to their entry into the database lay in the hands of the Länder (federal states), which as a rule make their entry dependent on an examination or a university degree.


The literature does not consider the quality of the translation to be sufficiently guaranteed by this: the conditions for entry in the databases vary in the various federal states, are formal and do not give any indication of the competence of the interpreter, especially in criminal proceedings; the court cannot control the translation work; in practice, the use of a sworn interpreter is sometimes dispensed with and instead, for example, a person brought by the accused is employed (Eisenberg, Juristische Rundschau 2013, 442, 447 et seq.; Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 189 GVG para. 4 et seqq.). However, it should be noted that the Directive does not specify how to determine the quality of the translation either (see the criticism by Siry, in: Allegrezza/Covolo (eds.), Effective Defence Rights in Criminal Proceedings, 2018, pp. 35, 41, 49 et seq).


In the meantime, the Federal legislator has created a uniform federal scheme in the form of the Court Interpreters Act, which, among other things, lays down qualification requirements. It will enter into force on 1st July 2021 and at least establish uniform nationwide standards for the qualification of interpreters.

items.heading: Article 3
items.subHeading: Right to translation of essential documents

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that suspected or accused persons who do not understand the language of the criminal proceedings concerned are, within a reasonable period of time, provided with a written translation of all documents which are essential to ensure that they are able to exercise their right of defence and to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings.

provisions.textEn:
(1) 1 The court shall provide an interpreter or a translator for an accused or convicted person who has no command of the German language insofar as this is necessary for the exercise of his rights under the law of criminal procedure. [...]

(2) 1As a rule, the exercise the procedural rights of the accused who has no command of the German language in criminal proceedings require a written translation of orders depriving him of his liberty, as well as of indictments, penalty orders and non-appealable judgments. 2An excerpt of a written translation is sufficient if the procedural rights of the accused in criminal proceedings are thereby safeguarded. 3The written translation must be made available to the accused without delay. [...]

provisions.comment: Section 37 (3) was introduced by the Act on strengthening the procedural rights of defendants in criminal proceedings (Gesetz zur Stärkung der Verfahrensrechte vonBeschuldigten im Strafverfahren) in order to implement Art. 3 of the Directive. The requirement of joint service of the judgment and the translation is intended to ensure that the time limits for giving reasons for an appeal do not begin to run at a time when the defendant is not yet able to understand the content of the judgment due to insufficient command of the language.
provisions.textEn: If a translation of the judgment is to be made available to a participant in the proceedings pursuant to section 187 (1) and (2) of the Courts Constitution Act, the judgment shall be served together with the translation. In such cases service on the other participants in the proceedings shall be effected at the same time as service pursuant to the first sentence.

items.comment: The German legislator has chosen a different wording regarding the documents that are to be translated (see also above, commentary on Art. 2 (1), (2)). The description 'insofar as this is necessary for the exercise of his procedural rights in criminal proceedings' corresponds more or less to the phrase 'which are essential to ensure that they are able to exercise their right of defence' from the directive, whereas alternative option 'which are essential to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings' does not have an equivalent in the German provisions. In abstract terms, it hardly seems possible that the withholding of a translation of a piece of information could impair procedural fairness without at the same time being relevant to the exercise of the procedural rights of the accused, at least his last word. However, it cannot be excluded that there may be different interpretations in this respect and that in this case German law is interpreted more narrowly (see also the criticism by Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para. 7)

items.text: 2. Essential documents shall include any decision depriving a person of his liberty, any charge or indictment, and any judgment.

provisions.textEn: 1As a rule, the exercise the procedural rights of the accused who has no command of the German language in criminal proceedings require a written translation of orders depriving him of his liberty, as well as of indictments, penalty orders and non-appealable judgments. 2An excerpt of a written translation is sufficient if the procedural rights of the accused in criminal proceedings are thereby safeguarded. 3The written translation must be made available to the accused without delay.

nationalActs.title: Richtlinien für das Strafverfahren und das Bußgeldverfahren
nationalActs.titleEn: Directives on criminal and administrative fine proceedings

provisions.textEn: Summonses, arrest warrants, penal orders, bills of indictment and other court decisions on the merits of the case must be notified to the foreigner who does not have a sufficient command of the German language, accompanied by a translation into a language he or she understands.

If a translation of the judgment is to be made available to a participant in the proceedings pursuant to section 187 (1) and (2) of the Courts Constitution Act, the judgment shall be served together with the translation. In such cases service on the other participants in the proceedings shall be effected at the same time as service pursuant to the first sentence.

items.comment:
A. Section 187 (2) 1 CCA

Section 187 (2) 1 CCA deviates from the wording of the Directive in several respects and is therefore criticised as inadequate transposition.


I. Generic term for the documents to be translated

It is criticised that the legislator has not adopted the term 'essential documents', but instead refers to whether the translation is 'necessary for the exercise of the suspect's rights in criminal proceedings'. The necessity could only be estimated ex ante with difficulty, particularly from the perspective of the judge (Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para. 24).


II. Ambiguous legal presumtion

Section 187 (2) 1 precedes the list of documents to be translated with the phrase 'as a rule' and it is not clear how this phrase is to be understood (see also Schneider, Strafverteidiger 2015, 379 et seq., 383). On the one hand, it can be understood restrictively in the sense that the expressly named documents are only as a rule necessary for the exercise the procedural rights and therefore to be translated. Accordingly a translation might be dispensed with in exceptional cases, for example if an extract in accordance with sentence 2 or an oral translation in accordance with sentence 4 is sufficient. On the other hand, a broader interpretation is possible in the sense that (only) the documents mentioned are to be translated in any event, but in exceptional cases others might be necessary for the exercise the procedural rights and therefore to be translated as well.

The legislative materials (Bt-Drs. 17/12578, p. 11) are also unclear in this respect. The restrictive understanding might be backed up by the legal context with the exemptions from the rule. The broad interpretation, on the other hand, is supported by the fact, that German law would otherwise fall short of the guarantees of the Directive which it is intended to implement. According to the obligation to interpret national law in accordance with the Directives, the broad interpretation should be followed (see also Schneider, Strafverteidiger 2013, 389, 383 et seq.).


III. Restriction to non-appealable judgments

The German legislator has expressly limited the right to translation to non-appealable judgments and considers this to be in conformity with the Directive, as the temporal scope of application of the Directive as set out in Art. 2 (1) only extends to the conclusion of the proceedings (BT-Drucks. 17/12578, p. 11). According to Schneider, as already mentioned in the commentary to Art. 2 (1) of the Directive, this understanding was to narrow. She argues that in European law the right of appeal is not to be understood technically and can also cover extraordinary legal remedies (Schneider, Strafverteidiger 2015, 379, 380 et seq.; approvingly Frister, in: Systematischer Kommentar zur Strafprozessordnung Bd. IX, 5th ed. 2016, § 187 GVG para. 11; Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para.18; see also Mansdörfer/Schmitt, in: Allegrezza/Covolo (eds.), Effective Defence Rights in Criminal Proceedings, 2018, p. 295, 316). The temporal scope of application of the Directive thus extends beyond the force of law; the defendant must therefore also be able to demand a translation of final judgments, which is why the German law falls short of the protection guaranteed by the Directive.


IV. Restriction to judgments in the strict sense

It is also pointed out that the concept of judgment as used in the Directive is to be understood broadly, whereas German law limits the general obligation to translate judgments in the strict sense. The general obligation to translate therefore does not cover decisions terminating proceedings apart from judgments in the narrow sense and penal orders ('Strafbefehl') , e.g. 'Beschlüsse' (Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para.18), which e.g. are issued under section 206a Code of Criminal Procedure if a final obstacle to proceedings becomes apparent after the opening of the main proceedings but before the main hearing is held.

A corresponding obligation is indeed laid down in the Directives on criminal and administrative fine proceedings (Richtlinien für das Strafverfahren und das Bußgeldverfahren, RiStBV). Yet, the RiStBV are administrative regulations without legal force. They are issued by the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, are primarily aimed at the public prosecutor's office and the police and are intended to ensure a uniform approach in the relevant procedures.


Therefore, an interpretation in line with the Directive is suggested, which is based on the concept of essentiality and focuses on the meaning of the individual document (Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 GVG para. 19; Schneider, Strafverteidiger 2015, 379, 383 et seq.)


B. Section 187 (2) 2 CCA

The fact that the section 187 (2) 2 CCA requires only an excerpt to be translated, if the procedural rights of the accused in criminal proceedings are thereby safeguarded, is compatible with the protection guaranteed by the Directive only if that possibility is not used to dispense with a full translation, which would otherwise be required under the first sentence. Such an approach should again be countered with the obligation to interpret national law in accordance with the Directive.

items.text: 3. The competent authorities shall, in any given case, decide whether any other document is essential. Suspected or accused persons or their legal counsel may submit a reasoned request to that effect.
items.comment: It is standard practice for the competent court to appoint the interpreter or translator ex officio and it is recognised that the defendant is entitled to make a corresponding request (Rosenau, in: Satzger/Schluckebier/Widmaier, Strafprozessordnung, 4th ed. 2020, § 187 GVG para. 9 with further references).

items.text: 4. There shall be no requirement to translate passages of essential documents which are not relevant for the purposes of enabling suspected or accused persons to have knowledge of the case against them.

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: No need for implementation apparent.

items.text: 5. Member States shall ensure that, in accordance with procedures in national law, suspected or accused persons have the right to challenge a decision finding that there is no need for the translation of documents or passages thereof and, when a translation has been provided, the possibility to complain that the quality of the translation is not sufficient to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings.
items.comment: The accused may file a complaint or appeal against the judgement as already mentioned above in the commentary on Art. 2 (5). However, for a appeal on points of law to be successful, the judgment must be based on the incorrect translation.

items.text: 6. In proceedings for the execution of a European arrest warrant, the executing Member State shall ensure that its competent authorities provide any person subject to such proceedings who does not understand the language in which the European arrest warrant is drawn up, or into which it has been translated by the issuing Member State, with a written translation of that document.

nationalActs.title: Gesetz über die internationale Rechtshilfe in Strafsachen
nationalActs.titleEn: Act on International Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters

provisions.comment: See the commentary on the implementation of Art. 2 (7) above.
provisions.textEn: Unless this Act contains special procedural provisions, the provisions of the Courts Constitution Act and its Introductory Act, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Juvenile Courts Act, the Fiscal Code and the Administrative Offences Act shall apply accordingly.

items.text: 7. As an exception to the general rules established in paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 6, an oral translation or oral summary of essential documents may be provided instead of a written translation on condition that such oral translation or oral summary does not prejudice the fairness of the proceedings.

provisions.comment:
The presumption in section 187 (2) 5 CCA, that the procedural rights of the accused are also safeguarded in the case of a mere oral translation or oral summary of the contents of the documents if the accused has a defence counsel, has no equivalent in the Directive and considerably restricts the protection intended in it. The legislator assumed that, in principle, consultation with the defence counsel already enabled the accused person without command of the language to exercise his right of defence and sufficiently ensured a fair trial; it would also avoid delaying the proceedings by providing a written translation of the judgment after the written grounds of the judgment have been drafted. An exception was to be made where the defendant had a legitimate interest in a written translation which he could express by requesting it (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 17/12578, p. 12).


This deviation from the Directive is rightly considerably criticised in the literature. Section 187 (2) 5 reverses the relationship of rule and exception as laid down in Directive. Also, the defense counsel usually does not have sufficient factual knowledge to compensate for the reduction of information. Furthermore, it is not compatible with the fact that the accused has a right to translation of even the communication with the defence counsel. Finally the shift to the lawyer is also contrary to the principle that the translation should be free of charge regardless of the outcome of the proceedings (Bockemühl, StV 2014, 537, 538 f.;Eisenberg, Juristische Rundschau 2013, 442, 445; Mansdörfer/Schmitt, in: Allegrezza/Covolo (eds.), Effective Defence Rights in Criminal Proceedings, 2018, p. 295, 317; Oğlakcıoğlu, in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 187 para.19; Schneider, Strafverteidiger 2015, 379, 382).
provisions.textEn: 4 The written translation may be replaced by an oral translation of the documents or an oral summary of the content of the documents if the accused's rights under criminal procedure are thereby safeguarded. 5 As a rule, this is to be assumed if the accused has a defence counsel.

items.text: 8. Any waiver of the right to translation of documents referred to in this Article shall be subject to the requirements that suspected or accused persons have received prior legal advice or have otherwise obtained full knowledge of the consequences of such a waiver, and that the waiver was unequivocal and given voluntarily.

provisions.comment: Although the legislator was guided by the wording of the Directive when creating the provision, it opted for more far-reaching protection: The possibility of waiver presupposes an instruction; knowledge by other means is not sufficient. Moreover it is limited to the written translation, so that oral translation according to section 187 (2) 4 CCA cannot be waived. The protection afforded by national law therefore goes beyond the requirements of Article 3 (8) of the Directive. In contrast, the requirements of unambiguity and freedom from coercion are not explicitly laid down, but are implied.
provisions.textEn: The accused may only effectively waive a written translation if he has been instructed beforehand concerning his right to a written translation pursuant to subsections (1) and (2) and concerning the consequences of a waiver of a written translation.

items.text: 9. Translation provided under this Article shall be of a quality sufficient to safeguard the fairness of the proceedings, in particular by ensuring that suspected or accused persons have knowledge of the case against them and are able to exercise their right of defence.
items.comment: Translators are usually appointed by the use of a interpreter and translator database. For further details see the commentary on Art. 2 (8).

items.text: Member States shall meet the costs of interpretation and translation resulting from the application of Articles 2 and 3, irrespective of the outcome of the proceedings.
items.heading: Article 4

provisions.textEn: The court shall advise the accused in a language he understands that he may to this extent demand that an interpreter or a translator be called in for the entire criminal proceedings free of charge.

items.comment:
The cost of an interpreter a translator engaged by the court on behalf of the defendant are in principle borne by the treasury (section 464c CCP in conjunction with No. 9005 para. 4 List of costs of the CCA). If the accused has engaged the services of an interpreter or translator himself and if this was necessary for the exercise of his criminal procedural rights, the costs incurred thereby are to be reimbursed as well. It is acknowledged that costs may not be imposed on the suspect, even with hindsight (Eisenberg, Juristische Rundschau 2013, 442, 443; ECtHR, Luedicke, Belkacem and Koç v Germany, Application no. 6210/73; 6877/75; 7132/75, 28/11/1978, para 38 et seqq.; AG Tiergarten, NJW 1978, 2462).

The aforementioned assumption of costs can be read indirectly from the wording of the duty to inform according to section 187 (1) 2 CCA.

items.heading: Article 5
items.subHeading: Quality of the interpretation and translation

items.text: 1. Member States shall take concrete measures to ensure that the interpretation and translation provided meets the quality required under Article 2(8) and Article 3(9).
items.comment: See the commentary on Art. 2 (8) as to the appointment of interpreters and translators as well as their swearing in.

items.text: 2. In order to promote the adequacy of interpretation and translation and efficient access thereto, Member States shall endeavour to establish a register or registers of independent translators and interpreters who are appropriately qualified. Once established, such register or registers shall, where appropriate, be made available to legal counsel and relevant authorities.
items.comment: The Federal State Justice Administrations have created a database of interpreters and translators, which contains information on the interpreters and translators who are sworn, publicly appointed or generally authorised in the individual Federal states. It is accessible via http://www.justiz-dolmetscher.de/ (as of 13th April 2020).

items.text: 3. Member States shall ensure that interpreters and translators be required to observe confidentiality regarding interpretation and translation provided under this Directive.

provisions.textEn: The interpreter or translator shall observe secrecy concerning circumstances that become known to him in his professional capacity. The court shall advise him of this fact.

items.comment:
According to the legislative will and the prevailing opinion (see the legislative materials, BT-Drs. 17/1224, p. 10; Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 189 para. 4), the provision is a purely regulatory, procedural provision ('Soll-Vorschrift'), meaning, that it does not itself impose any obligations on the interpreter or the translator and that violations cannot be brought forward in an appeal on points of law. This is criticised by Oğlakcıoğlu (in: Münchener Kommentar zur StPO Bd. 3, 2018, § 189 GVG para. 22) with regards to the Directive, who argues that the obligation of confidentiality is supposed to serve the quality of the service as much as the swearing-in according to paragraph (1).


In some federal states, the laws on interpreting and translation services contain a genuine obligation of confidentiality.

items.text: Without prejudice to judicial independence and differences in the organisation of the judiciary across the Union, Member States shall request those responsible for the training of judges, prosecutors and judicial staff involved in criminal proceedings to pay special attention to the particularities of communicating with the assistance of an interpreter so as to ensure efficient and effective communication.
items.heading: Article 6

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: No regulations on training within the meaning of the Directive could be identified.

items.text: Member States shall ensure that when a suspected or accused person has been subject to questioning or hearings by an investigative or judicial authority with the assistance of an interpreter pursuant to Article 2, when an oral translation or oral summary of essential documents has been provided in the presence of such an authority pursuant to Article 3(7), or when a person has waived the right to translation pursuant to Article 3(8), it will be noted that these events have occurred, using the recording procedure in accordance with the law of the Member State concerned.
items.heading: Article 7

provisions.textEn: The instruction pursuant to the first sentence [regarding the right to a written translation under paragraphs 1 and 2 and on the consequences of waiving a written translation] and the waiver of the accused shall be documented.
A record shall be made of each judicial investigatory act.

The record must indicate the place and date of the hearing as well as the names of the persons who were involved and participated and must state whether the essential procedural formalities were observed.

(2) The examination of the accused, witnesses and experts shall be recorded pursuant to sections 168 and 168a insofar as this can be done without considerably delaying the investigations. If no record is made of the accused’s examination, the fact that his defence counsel participated in the examination shall be documented.

(3) The instruction of the accused prior to his examination pursuant to section 136 (1) and section 163a shall be documented.
A record shall be taken of the main hearing [...].
The record must substantially reflect the course and results of the main hearing and show that all essential formalities were observed [...].

items.comment:
The requirement of documentation is expressly regulated only with regard to the instruction about the right to written translation and the possibility of waiver, as well as with regard to the waiver itself.

Otherwise, the requirement arises from the general rules on the documentation of pre-trial hearings and the recording of the trial. According to these, the essential formalities of the hearing must be recorded, which also includes the use of an interpreter (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 17/12578, p. 10; Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, StPO, 62nd ed. 2019, § 185 GVG para. 7). For hearings by judges and public prosecutors, this was already regulated before the implementation of the Directive; for hearings by other investigating authorities, in particular the police, this was done in order to implement the Directive by extending section 168b CCP (see the legislative materials, BT-Drs. 17/12578, p. 17).
